title: Teen Dies From Brain-Eating Amoeba After Exposure at North Carolina Water Feature

body_markdown:
**A teenager in North Carolina has died from a rare brain infection caused by *Naegleria fowleri* , with state health officials saying a man-made water feature at a Durham community organization was the most likely source of exposure. The water feature had not completed the required permitting process, according to local health officials.**


A North Carolina teenager died after developing a rare and usually fatal brain infection caused by *Naegleria fowleri* , commonly known as the "brain-eating amoeba."


The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services said on Sept. 15 that its investigation identified a water feature at El Futuro, a community-based organization in Durham, as the most likely source of the teenager's exposure. However, officials emphasized that the investigation could not conclusively establish exactly where the infection occurred.


The case has drawn attention to the dangers associated with warm freshwater and the importance of proper maintenance and disinfection of recreational water features.


## Teen Came Into Contact With Water Feature


According to the North Carolina investigation, the teenager came into contact with the water feature during the likely exposure period and splashed water onto his face.


The teen later developed a severe headache and was hospitalized. He ultimately died after developing primary amebic meningoencephalitis, or PAM, the serious brain infection associated with *Naegleria fowleri* .


NCDHHS investigated several possible locations where the teenager could have encountered warm freshwater. These included the water feature at El Futuro, an apartment pool in Orange County, and two ponds in Alamance County.


Testing did not detect *Naegleria fowleri* at the other locations, making them less likely sources of exposure. State investigators, working with local health officials and experts from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, concluded that the El Futuro water feature was the most likely source based on the available epidemiological, laboratory and environmental evidence.


## Testing Found Evidence of the Amoeba


The investigation found *Naegleria fowleri* DNA in water collected from the water feature's storage tank.


Investigators also observed algae throughout portions of the man-made creek. Organic material and debris were found covering the feature's filter, conditions that raised concerns about the quality and maintenance of the recirculating water system.


The feature used a pump, recirculated water and several fountains.


NCDHHS said the water feature was closed by the Durham County Department of Health on Aug. 28, 2026. It remains closed to the public.


According to information provided to local media by Durham County officials, El Futuro had not completed the application, evaluation and permitting process required for the water feature.


El Futuro said it had cleaned the creek using power washing and had added chlorine by hand. The organization has also expressed condolences to the teenager's family and said it would continue cooperating with public health officials.


## What Is *Naegleria fowleri* ?


*Naegleria fowleri* is a microscopic, free-living amoeba that naturally occurs in warm freshwater and soil.


The organism has earned the nickname "brain-eating amoeba" because, in extremely rare circumstances, it can enter the body through the nose and travel to the brain. There it can cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis, a rapidly progressing infection that damages brain tissue.


The CDC says the infection is extremely rare. From 1962 through 2024, 167 cases were reported in the United States, with only four survivors. More recent CDC data show that 180 cases were diagnosed nationally from 1937 through 2025.


Despite the severity of the infection, the overall risk to individuals remains very low.


The amoeba does not normally cause infection simply because contaminated water is swallowed. The important route of infection is water containing the organism entering the nose.


There is also no evidence that *Naegleria fowleri* infection spreads from one person to another.


## Symptoms Can Progress Quickly


Early symptoms of PAM can resemble other forms of meningitis or serious illness.


According to the CDC, symptoms can include headache, fever, nausea and vomiting. Symptoms generally begin around five days after exposure, although the incubation period can range from one to 12 days.


As the infection progresses, patients can develop a stiff neck, confusion, difficulty paying attention, seizures, hallucinations and coma. Death typically occurs within several days after symptoms begin, although the progression can vary.


Because PAM is so uncommon and its early symptoms can resemble more common illnesses, diagnosis can be difficult.


Anyone who develops sudden symptoms such as severe headache, fever, vomiting or a stiff neck after recent exposure to warm freshwater should seek emergency medical attention, particularly if water may have entered the nose.


## How Can People Reduce the Risk?


The CDC recommends several precautions for people who participate in activities involving warm freshwater.


People can reduce the possibility of water entering the nose by holding their nose shut or using a nose clip when jumping or diving. Keeping the head above water in naturally hot water is also recommended.


The CDC advises avoiding activities in warm freshwater when temperatures are high and avoiding stirring up sediment in shallow water because *Naegleria fowleri* can live in sediment.


Properly maintained and adequately disinfected swimming pools present a different risk profile. The CDC says people do not get PAM from swimming in a properly maintained and disinfected pool. However, recreational water facilities that are inadequately maintained or insufficiently disinfected have rarely been associated with infections.


The organism can also be associated with contaminated water used for nasal rinsing. For nasal irrigation, the CDC recommends using distilled, sterile or appropriately boiled water rather than untreated tap water.


## A Rare but Serious Infection


The North Carolina case underscores the unusual circumstances in which *Naegleria fowleri* can cause disease.


The teenager's exposure occurred at a man-made water feature rather than a natural lake or river. State investigators found environmental and laboratory evidence linking the feature to the case, but they have not said that the precise point of exposure can be proven.


For the public, health officials continue to emphasize that *Naegleria fowleri* infections remain exceptionally rare.


The tragedy also highlights why recreational water systems require appropriate maintenance, monitoring and disinfection. In this case, the water feature remains closed while the investigation and public health response continue.


For families and communities, understanding how the infection occurs can help put the risk into perspective. Avoiding warm freshwater activities that allow water to enter the nose, following local closure notices and maintaining recreational water properly are among the measures recommended by public health authorities.


### Source


North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, "NCDHHS Shares Update on Rare Brain Infection Source," Sept. 15, 2026.
